question: Which statement best describes Windowing?
options: Since most rows aren't in the DOM, the scroll container must still represent the full list height so the scrollbar size and position are correct. A spacer element sized to total * rowHeight fakes that height, and rows are absolutely positioned at top = index * rowHeight inside it. Forgetting the spacer is the classic bug where the list 'collapses' to one screen because scrollTop can never grow large enough to reveal later rows.

With fixed-height rows, any row's position is pure math (index * rowHeight), so the visible range and total height are trivial to compute. Variable heights are far harder: you don't know a row's height until it renders, so the virtualizer must estimate up front, measure after layout (often via ResizeObserver), and maintain an offset cache it can binary-search. Mismatched estimates are what cause the dreaded 'scroll jump' when measured heights shift the offsets below.

Overscan renders a few extra rows just above and below the visible window so rows are already mounted before they scroll into view. Without it, fast scrolling can expose blank gaps for a frame because new rows haven't been painted yet. The tradeoff is straightforward: more overscan reduces flicker but mounts more nodes, so 1-5 rows is the usual sweet spot.

Windowing is the core idea of virtualization: render only the slice of rows currently inside the viewport instead of the whole list. It matters because browser layout, paint, and memory all scale with DOM node count, so a 50,000-row list becomes O(visible) work instead of O(N). Mechanically, the component derives the visible index range from the scroll offset and a known row height, then mounts only those rows.

Virtualization keys everything off the scroll container's scrollTop (the offset) and its visible height. An onScroll handler reads scrollTop into state, React recomputes the window, and the rendered slice swaps. The handler must stay cheap — read the offset, set state, let React render — because heavy work on every scroll event blocks the main thread and drops frames.

question: Which statement best describes The spacer / total height?
options: Off-screen rows simply don't exist in the DOM, so native find-in-page (Ctrl+F), screen-reader traversal, and most crawlers can't see them. This is a real cost of virtualization that must be recovered at the app level: an in-app search/filter over the full dataset, ARIA grid semantics (role=grid, aria-rowcount) so assistive tech knows the true size, and sometimes server-side pagination. Senior engineers weigh this rather than virtualizing every list reflexively.

Hand-rolled scroll math is full of edge cases — resize, RTL, sticky headers, nested scroll, variable heights — so production code should use a maintained library like react-window (FixedSizeList/VariableSizeList) or TanStack Virtual. They handle measurement, overscan, and edge cases for you. Understanding the underlying math still matters so you can debug and configure them correctly.

Virtualization only bounds rendering cost — it does not reduce how much data you fetch. For effectively unbounded datasets you pair windowing with cursor-based pagination or streaming, fetching the next page as the visible window nears the loaded edge and rendering skeleton placeholders for unloaded ranges. An LRU cache of pages keeps client memory bounded even if the user scrolls through millions of rows.
